text: You now know how to build a tensor product and compute one by hand. This lesson zooms out to what those tensor products build, collectively: the full state space a real multi-qubit quantum computer lives in — and why its size is the single biggest reason quantum computers are hard to simulate classically.

Two qubits combine via the tensor product into a basis of ket-zero-zero, ket-zero-one, ket-one-zero, ket-one-one — 4 basis vectors, matching 2 squared exactly. A general 2-qubit state is any combination of these 4 basis vectors, alpha, beta, gamma, delta, with the sum of their squared magnitudes equal to 1 — 4 genuinely independent numbers, not 2 numbers reused twice.

Each additional qubit tensors in another factor of 2. One qubit gives 2 dimensions, two qubits give 4, three give 8, ten give 1,024, and by 50 qubits the dimension count is already over a quadrillion. Each row simply doubles the one above it — that's exactly what exponential growth means in concrete terms.

A classical computer simulating a quantum state has to store one complex number per dimension. For 50 qubits, that's roughly a quadrillion complex numbers — already past what any current supercomputer's memory can hold, and it doubles again for every single additional qubit. A classical n-bit register needs only n bits to describe fully; an n-qubit register's general state needs 2 to the n amplitudes — completely different growth rates, and that gap is the whole reason classical simulation becomes intractable.

Next lesson tackles the piece of this story that makes the space genuinely strange: entanglement, described with a lot of mystical language, but underneath it all, an exact and checkable mathematical definition built directly from the tensor product.
